analysis.one_liner: Bans imports of fish from Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea until they end driftnet fishing.
analysis.headline: The driftnet import ban, backed by 32 House cosponsors from both parties, never received a vote in either committee it was sent to and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Commerce Department to determine whether Japan, Taiwan, or South Korea allowed their fishing fleets to use large driftnets, nets that hang in the water and catch everything that swims into them, including protected marine animals. If a country did, imports of its fish and marine animal products would be banned until the practice stopped. The bill never received a vote in either House committee it was sent to and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. commercial fishermen who compete against fish caught cheaply with destructive driftnets, coastal communities dependent on fishing, and the public that shares the ocean's fish, seabirds, dolphins, and other marine life that driftnets catch and kill unintentionally. If the import ban changed the three countries' practices, the open ocean's marine life would be the main beneficiary.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. fishermen, coastal communities, ocean conservation

how_it_helps.text: Would cut off the U.S. market for fish caught by driftnets, an efficient but destructive fishing method that catches and kills large amounts of non-target marine life, including the fish, marine mammals, and other animals the bill requires the Secretary to list.

Would give U.S. fishermen an economic reason for Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea to end the practice, since those fleets would lose access to American consumers until they prohibited driftnet fishing by their registered vessels.

Would force a decision quickly: within 180 days of enactment the Commerce Secretary would have to make an initial determination on each of the three countries and publish the list of species caught in driftnets.
Would piggyback on an existing law, the Fishermen's Protective Act of 1967, using its established certification and prohibition procedures rather than building a new enforcement system.

analysis.who_pays: Seafood importers, processors, and retailers who sell Japanese, Taiwanese, or Korean fish would bear the cost of losing the U.S. market, and consumers could face higher prices or less choice on some imported seafood. The three countries' fishing fleets would lose access to U.S. sales until they stopped driftnet fishing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Seafood importers, processors, and fishing fleets

drawbacks.text: The import ban is a blunt trade weapon: it would raise prices or reduce choices for U.S. seafood consumers and could invite trade retaliation from three major trading partners over a conservation dispute.
The State Department gave the bill an unfavorable executive comment, reflecting the diplomatic and trade friction the administration saw in threatening major allies with an import ban.

The ban only takes effect if the Commerce Secretary formally determines a country still allows driftnet fishing, leaving room for the determination to be deferred or softened through diplomatic pressure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have used American buying power to pressure three countries into ending a fishing practice that wastes ocean life, a goal U.S. fishermen and ocean users broadly share. The cost is real but narrower: higher prices or less availability on some imported seafood and friction with three major trading partners. The larger weakness is design, not cost — the ban hinges entirely on a discretionary Commerce Department determination and a single unfavorable administration view, as the State Department's comment showed, could stall it in practice even if the law passed. Weighing all of that, the environmental and fishing-industry benefits outweighed the consumer cost, though the bill died before anyone had to make that trade-off in the open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees, drew an unfavorable comment from the State Department, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 19, 1989, and referred the same day to two House committees, Ways and Means and Merchant Marine and Fisheries.

It was divided between a trade subcommittee and a fisheries and wildlife subcommittee, and executive branch comment was requested from State, Commerce, the Marine Mammal Commission, and Transportation.
The Department of State sent unfavorable executive comment on May 1, 1990.
No committee vote, markup, or floor action followed, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign fishing fleets using driftnets and the seafood importers who bring their catch to the U.S. market were better off, because access to American buyers never closed. U.S. fishermen and the marine life the bill aimed to protect got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign driftnet fishing fleets and seafood importers

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 31 cosponsors across both parties

for.name: Reps. Jolene Unsoeld, Les Aucoin, and John Miller of Washington
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee and House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration or a vote before the Congress ended

against.name: U.S. Department of State
against.what_they_did: Delivered unfavorable executive comment on the bill to the House

sides.party_line_note: Support was small but bipartisan — 29 of 257 House Democrats and 3 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored — and no vote ever took place that would have split the parties.

industries.industry: Driftnet fishing fleets of Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea
industries.note: These fleets used large drifting nets that catch and kill huge quantities of non-target marine life. The bill would cut off their access to the U.S. market until they stopped, so their interest ran against the conservation goal.

Their business depends on continuing to bring foreign-caught fish into the country. An import ban would interrupt that supply, and their interest in keeping the market open ran against the bill's conservation purpose.

The bill would remove competition from fish caught with methods that deplete shared ocean resources and kill marine mammals and other non-target species. Its sponsors came largely from Pacific Northwest fishing districts.
